source.title: Depth-Dependent Safety Geometry in Vision-Language Models: Layer-Wise Localization and Bidirectional Refusal Control
source.authors: M. Karamat; Syed Talal Hassan; Christian García

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a layer-specific harmful-minus-safe mean-difference direction causally changes refusal, using activation steering in selected vision-encoder layers of a VLM rather than the original residual-stream ablation and addition procedure.
record.gate_note: The study reports layer-wise divergence and a projection plot to characterize or select candidate layers; those are not behavioral outcomes. The activation-scaling tables and MMLU result concern magnitude scaling, not intervention on the difference-in-means direction, so they are not included as rows for the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study builds a layer-specific unsafe-minus-safe mean-difference direction in Qwen3-VL-4B's vision encoder and measures how steering along it changes refusal rates (Table 3). That is a causal test of V1 in a new setting, a VLM vision tower, using projection-scaling steering rather than the original residual-stream ablation and addition.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that early vision layers (7–10) of Qwen3-VL-4B allow strong bidirectional refusal control via global directional steering (URR 6%–96%). Later layers (18–20/18–22) barely respond to steering but react to magnitude scaling, reaching 96% URR at the cost of high false refusal. Representational separability does not imply causal controllability. InternVL2.5-4B shows similar geometry only representationally, and the attack surface is white-box, not input-level.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a harmful-minus-safe layer-specific mean-difference direction, but steers selected visual-token activations in a frozen VLM; it does not perform the original all-layer residual-stream ablation or addition.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer region, steering scope (focused versus global), and steering strength change the outcome; early and later vision layers show different responses.

fits_no_version.finding: Uniform magnitude scaling of all visual-token activations shifts refusal strongly. At α=0.85 in vision layers 7–10, URR and SRR both reach 100% on UnsafeBench. At α=1.15 in layers 18–22, URR is 96% and SRR 91%. These scalings are not along the refusal direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal in VLMs is sensitive to non-directional activation magnitude in vision layers, with a depth-dependent asymmetry.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Foundations of Language Model Security
record.problems: Directional interventions are reported only for Qwen3-VL-4B; the other model receives representational analysis only. The interventions require white-box access and do not establish that external inputs can realize the shifts. MMLU utility is checked for magnitude scaling, not for directional steering, and uses 100 samples. No uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 1 and 2 report activation magnitude scaling by layer region and strength, plus the text reports a 100-sample MMLU result. These do not intervene on the difference-in-means direction and were therefore left out of the version-linked rows.

untested.parts: No ablation of the direction across all residual-stream layers and positions of the language model. Only scaling of the projected component in selected vision-encoder layers is tested. No capability check under directional steering: MMLU was run only for magnitude scaling.
No jailbreak analysis and no adversarial training.
No comparison of single versus multi-dimensional structure; higher-dimensional subspaces are named as future work.
InternVL2.5-4B gets divergence analysis only. No direction transfer is tested.

record.verdict_notes: Several values in the 18–20 focused rows were taken from the adjacent global column (S44, S48) or misread (S25, S37, S38, S47). The steering operation is h + α·proj(h), so α=-1 equals ablation and α<-1 flips the component. Under that reading, the paper's 'bidirectional control' runs opposite to V1's sign at large |α|. The direction is unnormalized relative to the token mean, so sign semantics may be confounded. Results are single-run with no uncertainty, and the sample sizes for URR and SRR in Table 3 are not stated. The tranche is set to T3 rather than T2 because the intervention site is a vision encoder, a new setting.

versions.untested_parts: Tests directional steering only in selected Qwen3-VL-4B vision layers and visual tokens. Does not ablate the direction from every residual-stream layer and position; does not test directional steering on general capability.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration.
No external jailbreak test showing attacks suppress the direction, and no training against its ablation.
No comparison of a single direction with an affine subspace, cone, or multiple refusal directions.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.
InternVL2.5-4B is analyzed for layer-wise divergence, but the learned direction is not transferred or causally tested across models; no language or base-to-instruct transfer test.
No comparison of refusal-training methods, timing, or stages.

relationships.condition: Qwen3-VL-4B vision layers 7–10, global steering on all visual tokens
relationships.reason: The direction strongly controls refusal (URR 6–96%), but not in V1's sign pattern. α=1 raises refusal (S03, S04), while α=2 and α=4 cut it (S05, S07, S08) and α=-4 raises it (S11, S12). URR and SRR also move together, so the control is not selective.
relationships.display_finding: URR ranged from 6% to 96%: α=1 and −4 raised refusal, while α=2 and 4 lowered it, with URR and SRR moving together.

relation.reason: Builds the unsafe-minus-safe direction and measures URR/SRR causally under steering at two layer bands and two token scopes.

tranche.reason: New setting: the vision encoder of a VLM, with a mean-difference direction built from unsafe vs safe images and projection-scaling steering. It reports refusal rates under the intervention (Table 3). It does not argue that V1 is wrong, so T5 does not fit.

source_check.notes: Steering is h+α(h·Ê)Ê on vision-encoder tokens: α=−1 would be ablation (untested) and α<−1 a flip. The text never states the sign of the per-token projection, so reading α>0 as "adding" is an assumption. Not stated for Table 3: refusal judge, n (all values even), random-direction control, output coherence. MMLU (100 items, 44%) was checked for magnitude scaling only. Unsteered baselines differ between tables: Table 1 URR 72/SRR 26 vs Table 3 84/32.

statements.correction: Qwen3-VL-4B, vision layers 7–10, global steering: URR 84→94 (α=1), 70 (α=2), 6 (α=4), 82 (α=−2), 96 (α=−4). Focused (CLS + 10 tokens): URR 82–84 at every α. Steering rescales each token's projection on the unsafe-minus-safe vision-encoder direction.
statements.problem: The numbers for this study are right. It leaves out that α=1 raised URR 84→94 (V1's sign), so the response is non-monotonic rather than simply reversed.

statements.correction: Layers 7–10 global: α=1 URR 84→94, SRR 32→60 (addition induces refusal); α=2 URR 70, SRR 44; α=4 URR 6, SRR 8 (reversal). Layers 18–20: URR 80–84 at all α. The intervention is h+α(h·Ê)Ê on visual tokens, not a fixed added vector.
statements.problem: 84%→6% is right only for α=4, global steering, layers 7–10. 'Positive α in vision layers' overstates it: α=1 induced refusal, and layers 18–20 did not respond.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Qwen3-VL-4B early vision layers 7–10, global steering
reader_labels.reason: Steering effects are strength-dependent: α = 2.0 produces only partial changes in both rejection rates, while α = 4.0 reduces unsafe rejection but also lowers safe rejection; opposite-direction α = -4.0 raises both rates. Focused steering is mostly near baseline (S01–S24).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: Unsafe rejection remains near baseline under tested directional steering, including global steering, despite projection separation being reported for deeper representations (S25–S48).
